structure.title: About the Federal Reserve
structure.summary:
iii
About the Federal Reserve
The Federal Reserve was created by an act of Congress on December 23, 1913, to provide the nation with a safer, more flexible, and more stable monetary and financial system. In establishing the Federal Reserve System, the United States was divided geographically into 12 Districts, each with a separately incorporated Reserve Bank.
For more information about the Federal Reserve Board and the Federal Reserve System, visit the Board’s website at https://www.federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/default.htm. Online versions of the Board’s annual report are available at https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/annual- report/default.htm.

structure.title: 1 Overview
structure.summary: The 2023 Federal Reserve Annual Report describes the System’s operations across monetary policy, financial stability, supervision and regulation, payment systems, and consumer protection and community development. It explains the Federal Reserve’s structure of 12 Reserve Banks and a seven-member Board of Governors, and provides appendixes covering leadership, FOMC meeting minutes, audited finances and oversight reviews, budgets and currency costs, policy actions, litigation, and historical operational statistics.

structure.title: 2 Monetary Policy and Economic Developments

nodes.title: March 2024 Summary
Recent Economic and Financial Developments
nodes.summary: The text reviews recent U.S. and international economic and financial developments and monetary policy. U.S. inflation has fallen markedly but remains above target, while longer-term expectations stay anchored. The labor market is still tight despite easing demand, with rising labor supply and moderating but elevated wage growth. Economic growth strengthened in 2023 through consumer spending and recovering housing activity, although business investment and manufacturing weakened. Financial conditions tightened after further policy-rate increases, credit became more expensive, and bank lending slowed. The banking system remains resilient, but elevated asset valuations, financial-sector leverage, asset losses, and rising funding costs pose risks. Foreign growth and inflation weakened unevenly, most foreign central banks paused tightening, and some began easing; the dollar rose slightly. The FOMC has held the federal funds rate at 5.25–5.50 percent since July and is awaiting greater confidence that inflation is sustainably returning to 2 percent before cutting rates.

nodes.title: Monetary Policy
nodes.summary: The text reviews financial stability, international economic and inflation developments, and U.S. monetary policy. The banking system is resilient but faces valuation, leverage, liquidity, and funding-cost risks. Foreign growth weakened and inflation declined unevenly, while many central banks paused hikes and some began easing. The FOMC has maintained a 5¼–5½ percent policy-rate target and requires greater confidence in sustained 2 percent inflation before cutting rates. The Federal Reserve is also reducing its securities holdings under its balance-sheet runoff plan, intending to stop when reserves remain consistent with an ample-reserves regime. Finally, the text highlights how the recent exceptionally tight labor market narrowed employment and wage disparities across demographic and educational groups, with some reaching historical lows in 2023.

nodes.title: Special Topics
nodes.summary: The text reviews interest-rate developments, the Federal Reserve's continued commitment to evaluate data, the outlook, and risks in setting the federal funds rate, and its ongoing balance-sheet reduction. It explains the scale and intended endpoint of securities runoff, then discusses special topics: improved but still unequal employment and earnings outcomes across demographic groups; how high mortgage rates, strong employment, remote work, limited existing-home supply, and new multifamily construction have shaped housing; changes in the Federal Reserve's balance sheet, reserves, and reverse-repurchase facility; and how easing inflation and improved labor-market balance have brought most simple policy-rule recommendations close to the current federal funds target range.

The section reviews U.S. and international economic developments, financial stability, and Federal Reserve monetary policy as of March 2024. Inflation has fallen considerably but remains above 2 percent, while employment, consumer spending, and GDP growth remain strong despite some weakness in business investment and manufacturing. The labor market is easing but still tight, with moderating wages and improved yet unequal outcomes across demographic groups. The FOMC has maintained a 5¼–5½ percent federal funds rate since July 2023 and awaits stronger evidence of sustainably lower inflation before cutting rates. Financial conditions have tightened, banking and financial-sector risks remain, and foreign growth and inflation have weakened unevenly as some central banks begin easing. The Federal Reserve continues balance-sheet runoff and assesses reserves, the reverse-repurchase facility, interest-rate developments, policy rules, and housing conditions shaped by mortgage rates, employment, remote work, limited home supply, and multifamily construction.

nodes.title: June 2023 Summary
Recent Economic and Financial Developments
nodes.summary: The June 2023 assessment found that U.S. inflation had declined but remained substantially above the 2 percent goal, with core services and wage pressures still elevated, while longer-term expectations remained anchored. The labor market was exceptionally strong but showed emerging signs of easing. Economic growth was modest, consumer and business activity were slowing under tighter financial conditions, and housing remained weak. The FOMC raised the federal funds rate to 5–5¼ percent, slowed the pace of increases, and continued reducing its securities holdings, stating that future decisions would depend on incoming data, cumulative tightening, and policy lags. Financial conditions tightened, credit growth slowed, and some delinquencies and default risks increased. The banking system remained resilient despite three bank failures and broader vulnerabilities in real estate, hedge funds, and certain funds. Foreign activity recovered early in the year, though momentum and inflation trends varied, and major foreign central banks generally continued tightening cautiously. The Federal Reserve stressed the hardship caused by inflation and its strong commitment to restoring price stability, likely through a period of below-trend growth and softer labor-market conditions.

nodes.title: Monetary Policy
nodes.summary: The text reviews financial, international, and U.S. monetary developments in 2023. Real estate and nonbank financial vulnerabilities remained notable, while three banks failed amid uninsured-deposit, interest-rate, and risk-management problems; the wider banking system nevertheless retained liquidity and loss-absorbing strength. Global activity recovered early in the year, inflation eased mainly through lower energy prices but food and core inflation stayed high, and foreign central banks generally continued tightening cautiously. The FOMC raised the federal funds rate to 5–5¼ percent and continued balance-sheet runoff, while evaluating further moves based on incoming data and the goal of 2 percent inflation. The text also discusses narrowing but persistent demographic employment and wage disparities, tighter bank lending and its potentially uneven economic effects, and the Federal Reserve’s March liquidity measures, including the BTFP, which increased total assets despite ongoing portfolio reduction.

nodes.title: Special Topics
nodes.summary: The text reviews Federal Reserve balance-sheet reduction and its partial offset by emergency bank lending, developments in employment and earnings disparities, tighter bank credit and its possible economic effects, and the roles of the BTFP, discount window, SOMA portfolio, and ON RRP facility in banking and money markets. It also explains that persistent above-target inflation and tight labor markets have caused simple monetary-policy rules to recommend elevated federal funds rates, while noting related Federal Reserve reports and sources.

The June 2023 summary examines U.S. inflation, labor markets, economic activity, housing, financial conditions, banking resilience, and international developments. It covers the FOMC’s rate increase to 5–5¼ percent, continued balance-sheet reduction, and data-dependent policy approach, alongside tighter credit, rising delinquency risks, bank failures, and vulnerabilities in nonbank finance and real estate. It also reviews foreign inflation and monetary tightening, employment and wage disparities, and the effects of tighter bank lending. Special attention is given to the BTFP, discount window, SOMA portfolio, and ON RRP facility, including how emergency lending partially offset balance-sheet runoff, as well as policy-rule indications for elevated rates and the Federal Reserve’s commitment to restoring 2 percent inflation despite expected economic and labor-market costs.

structure.summary: The section reviews U.S. and global economic and financial developments and Federal Reserve policy in June 2023 and March 2024. Inflation had fallen substantially but remained above 2 percent, while economic activity, consumer spending, employment, and GDP were resilient despite weakness in investment and manufacturing; labor markets were easing but still tight, with moderating wages and unequal demographic outcomes. The FOMC raised the federal funds rate to 5–¼ percent in June 2023 and maintained it at 5¼–5½ percent thereafter, continued balance-sheet reduction, and emphasized data dependence and the need for sustained disinflation before easing. The section also covers tighter credit and financial conditions, bank failures and resilience, delinquency, nonbank and real-estate vulnerabilities, emergency lending and Federal Reserve facilities, policy rules, reserves and the SOMA and ON RRP portfolios, housing pressures, and uneven foreign growth, inflation, and monetary-policy responses.

structure.title: 3 Financial Stability

nodes.title: Monitoring Financial Vulnerabilities
Asset Valuation Pressures
nodes.summary: The text explains the Federal Reserve’s financial-stability framework, distinguishing shocks from gradually developing vulnerabilities and describing quarterly monitoring of valuations, borrowing, financial-sector leverage, and funding risks to guide policy and coordination with domestic and international authorities. It discusses the Financial Stability Report and its transparency role, then assesses 2023 asset-valuation pressures: equities and real estate remained expensive relative to fundamentals, corporate spreads were relatively subdued, residential property valuations stayed historically high, commercial real estate prices remained elevated despite market weakness and low transactions, and farmland prices rose. It also introduces excessive household and business borrowing as a crisis vulnerability that can magnify shocks by forcing spending cuts, and includes figures, notes, and sources on equity valuation and corporate bond spreads.

nodes.title: Borrowing by Households and Businesses
nodes.summary: The text assesses financial stability in 2023. Equity, residential real estate, commercial real estate, and farmland valuations remained elevated relative to fundamentals, while corporate credit spreads were comparatively moderate. Household and business debt declined relative to GDP, and although business leverage and household delinquencies showed some weaknesses, earnings, fixed-rate borrowing, conservative lending, and pandemic-related student-loan measures limited stress. Private credit grew rapidly but remained difficult to assess because of limited transparency. The banking system was generally resilient, supported by strong capital ratios and emergency measures that contained the March 2023 bank-run episode, though fair-value losses, commercial real estate exposure, and vulnerabilities at smaller banks remained concerns. The figures document historical equity valuations, corporate spreads, private-sector credit-to-GDP, and bank capital ratios, with sources including Federal Reserve calculations, BEA data, Federal Reserve financial accounts, and ICE Data Indices.

nodes.title: Leverage in the Financial System
nodes.summary: The text reviews financial stability through household and financial-sector vulnerabilities in 2023. Private credit expanded but remained opaque; households retained strong balance sheets and declining debt-to-GDP despite modestly higher consumer delinquencies. Banks stayed resilient, with strong capital and liquidity, though the SVB-related turmoil highlighted risks from fair-value losses and fragile funding, while CRE exposure, interest-rate mismatches, and weaker smaller-bank diversification remain concerns. Life insurers and hedge funds faced investment and leverage risks, and nonbank liquidity vehicles, especially money market funds, continued to expand, prompting SEC reforms. The accompanying figures document bank capital ratios and liquid-asset levels by bank group, with definitions, recession shading, and Federal Reserve data sources.

nodes.title: Funding Risk
nodes.summary: The text reviews 2023 financial-stability risks outside and within banking, covering elevated hedge-fund leverage, rising life-insurer investment risk, generally ample but somewhat reduced bank liquidity, the expiration of the BTFP, and persistently high bank interest-rate exposure. It describes trends in bank liquid assets, MMFs and related cash vehicles, mutual-fund bond holdings, and stablecoins, including associated systemic vulnerabilities and regulatory developments. It then explains Federal Reserve cooperation and the FSOC's role, membership, systemic-risk responsibilities, 2023 priorities, and monitoring initiatives for hedge funds and nonbank mortgage servicers.

The section explains how the Federal Reserve monitors financial stability through quarterly assessments of asset valuations, household and business borrowing, financial-sector leverage, and funding risk, emphasizing the interconnectedness of financial institutions and the real economy and the ability of a stable system to withstand shocks. It reviews 2023 conditions, finding elevated equity and real-estate valuations, moderate corporate spreads, declining private-sector debt relative to GDP, and limited but emerging household and business credit stress. Banks remained broadly resilient because of strong capital, liquidity, and policy support, although fair-value losses, fragile funding, interest-rate mismatches, commercial real estate, smaller-bank weaknesses, and opaque private credit posed risks. The section also covers leverage and investment risks among hedge funds and life insurers; growth and vulnerabilities in money market funds, mutual funds, stablecoins, and other nonbank vehicles; regulatory responses; and Federal Reserve, FSOC, and broader domestic and international monitoring and coordination efforts, supported by figures and underlying data sources.

nodes.title: Domestic and International Cooperation and Coordination
Financial Stability Oversight Council Activities
nodes.summary: The text describes 2023 developments in financial stability, including declining corporate bond mutual-fund holdings, orderly redemptions, and persistent risks from largely unregulated stablecoins. It outlines Federal Reserve cooperation through the FSOC and FSB, explains the FSOC's mandate and 2023 priorities, and details its monitoring of nonbanks, Treasury markets, climate risks, and digital assets; its finalized risk-identification framework and nonbank designation guidance; and the subjects covered in its annual report. It concludes with the FSB's international work on open-end fund liquidity, crypto-asset intermediaries, and nonbank financial resilience.

Financial Stability Board Activities
In light of the interconnected global financial system and the global activities of large U.S. finan- cial institutions, the Federal Reserve participates in international bodies, such as the FSB. The FSB monitors the global financial system and promotes international financial stability by coordi- nating with national financial authorities and international standard-setting bodies on information exchanges and work focused on developing strong global financial-sector policies.
In 2023, the FSB engaged in many issues related to global financial stability. Specific work included addressing structural vulnerabilities from liquidity mismatch in open-end funds, assessing the financial stability implications of multifunction crypto-asset intermediaries, and enhancing the resilience of nonbank financial intermediation.

The section reviews domestic and international cooperation on financial stability in 2023. It covers the FSOC’s oversight mandate, priorities, risk monitoring, nonbank designation framework, and annual-report topics; Federal Reserve coordination with the FSOC, FSB, and other authorities; and the FSB’s global work on open-end fund liquidity, crypto-asset intermediaries, nonbank resilience, transaction and information-transfer technologies, and quantum computing.

structure.summary: The section describes how the Federal Reserve promotes financial stability by monitoring vulnerabilities, informing policy tools and stress tests, addressing risks from systemically important institutions, and coordinating with domestic and international authorities. It reviews 2023 conditions across markets, households, businesses, banks, insurers, hedge funds, and nonbank financial vehicles; evaluates resilience and emerging risks such as valuations, funding fragility, interest-rate mismatches, commercial real estate, private credit, and crypto-related activity; and summarizes related regulatory, FSOC, FSB, research, and international cooperation efforts.

structure.title: 4 Supervision and Regulation

nodes.title: Box 4.1. Banking Sector Conditions
nodes.summary: This section describes the Federal Reserve’s supervision and regulation mission, including promoting a safe, sound, efficient financial system; supervising institutions; developing regulatory policies and acting on banking applications; and monitoring the banking sector through data collection and analysis. It references the semiannual Supervision and Regulation Report on banking conditions and identifies the broad range of supervised entities, with their counts, including an explanation of Edge Act and agreement corporations.

nodes.title: Supervised and Regulated Institutions
State Member Banks
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s portfolio-based classification of supervised institutions and reports year-end 2023 statistics for member and state member banks. It gives total membership, state-chartered membership, branch coverage, and shares of U.S. commercial banks, offices, and insured assets, followed by a table categorizing LISCC, large and foreign, regional, community, and insurance or commercial holding-company organizations by definition, institution count, and total assets, with footnotes explaining the composition of selected totals.

nodes.title: Bank Holding Companies
nodes.summary: The text reports 2023 statistics on U.S. bank holding companies, financial holding companies, and savings and loan holding companies, including their numbers, ownership, assets, activities, and regulatory oversight. It also describes the Federal Reserve’s risk-based supervisory framework for insurance-focused SLHCs and its 2023 implementation, then introduces financial market utilities as multilateral systems for transferring, clearing, and settling financial transactions.

nodes.title: Savings and Loan Holding Companies
nodes.summary: The text reports 2023 statistics on U.S. bank holding companies, financial holding companies, and savings and loan holding companies, including their numbers, ownership, asset distributions, activities, and regulatory oversight. It also describes the Federal Reserve’s insurance-organization supervisory framework and its 2023 implementation, and begins defining financial market utilities as multilateral systems for transferring, clearing, and settling financial transactions.

nodes.title: Financial Market Utilities
nodes.summary: The text reviews Federal Reserve supervision and regulation of U.S. BHCs, SLHCs, insurance-focused holding companies, financial market utilities, and international banking activities. It provides 2023 counts, asset levels, ownership and regulatory details for BHCs, FHCs, SLHCs, and foreign banks; describes the Federal Reserve’s risk-based insurance supervisory framework and 2023 implementation; explains FMU supervision, the significance of eight Title VIII designations, and Regulation HH requirements; and reports U.S. banks’ foreign branches, Edge Act and agreement corporations, and foreign banks’ U.S. operations and share of commercial banking assets.

nodes.title: International Activities
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s oversight of designated and other financial market utilities, including its expanded systemic-risk responsibilities under Dodd-Frank and the requirements of Regulation HH. It reports 2023 international banking operations involving U.S. banks, Edge Act corporations, and foreign banks, along with related examination totals. It explains the Federal Reserve’s risk-based supervisory methods, priorities, and remediation focus, and details its response to the Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank failures, including findings on SVB’s vulnerabilities and efforts to strengthen supervision. It concludes with 2023 examination and inspection counts for state member banks, bank holding companies, and savings and loan holding companies.

The section surveys the Federal Reserve’s supervision and regulation of state member banks, bank holding companies, savings and loan holding companies, insurance-focused organizations, financial market utilities, and international banking operations. It presents 2023 institution counts, classifications, ownership, assets, activities, branch and market coverage, and examination data; explains risk-based supervisory frameworks, FMU oversight, Title VIII designations, and Regulation HH; describes international operations and related examinations; and discusses supervisory priorities, remediation, and lessons and responses arising from the Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank failures.

nodes.title: Supervisory Developments
Supervisory and Regulatory Initiatives
Specialized Examinations
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s specialized supervisory examinations and related regulatory responsibilities, including stress testing and capital planning, fiduciary and transfer-agent activities, government and municipal securities, securities-credit lenders, and operational resilience, information technology, and cybersecurity. It details the 2023 stress test results, capital-buffer implementation, exploratory and global market shocks, related publications, examination counts, applicable laws and rules, and the Federal Reserve’s resources for managing operational, cyber, and third-party risks.

nodes.title: Operational Resilience, Information Technology, and Cybersecurity
nodes.summary: The text reports the Federal Reserve’s 2023 examinations of fiduciary activities, transfer agents, government and municipal securities dealers, and securities-credit lenders. It describes efforts to strengthen operational resilience through guidance, outreach, IT and cybersecurity examinations, technology-service-provider oversight, domestic and international regulatory collaboration, incident reporting, and cloud-resilience initiatives. It also introduces the Novel Activities Supervision Program for crypto-assets, distributed ledger technology, and technology-based nonbank partnerships, and summarizes an interagency warning about key risks associated with crypto-assets and crypto-sector participants.

nodes.title: Crypto-Asset Supervision
nodes.summary: The text describes international guidance on third-party and cyber risks, the Federal Reserve's 2023 Novel Activities Supervision Program and its focus on crypto-assets, distributed ledgers, and technology-driven nonbank partnerships, as well as related interagency crypto-risk statements and the supervisory nonobjection process for dollar-token activities. It also covers the Federal Reserve's exploratory climate scenario analysis and finalized climate-risk management principles for large institutions, including their governance and risk-management scope. Finally, it introduces the Federal Reserve's enforcement authority and use of formal actions against unsafe practices and violations.

nodes.title: Climate-Related Financial Risks
nodes.summary: The text describes federal supervisory developments concerning crypto-asset liquidity and dollar-token activities, including a nonobjection process for state member banks and the associated operational, cybersecurity, liquidity, illicit-finance, and consumer-compliance risks. It then covers the Federal Reserve’s exploratory 2023 climate scenario analysis exercise and finalized climate-risk management principles for large institutions, addressing physical and transition risks across governance and traditional risk areas. Finally, it introduces the Federal Reserve’s enforcement authority over supervised institutions and affiliated parties, including formal cease-and-desist actions for unsafe practices or violations.

nodes.title: Enforcement Actions
nodes.summary: The text discusses Federal Reserve supervision and regulation of crypto-asset activities, climate-related financial risks, enforcement, bank disclosures, and appeals of supervisory decisions. It describes the 2023 dollar-token supervisory nonobjection process and related risk concerns; the exploratory climate scenario analysis and finalized climate-risk management principles for large institutions; the Federal Reserve’s formal and informal enforcement actions, penalties, and public disclosure practices; state member bank financial-reporting requirements; and the two-level internal process for appealing material supervisory determinations.

nodes.title: Internal Appeals of Material Super visory Determinations
nodes.summary: The text reports the Federal Reserve’s 2023 enforcement, disclosure, supervisory appeals, assessment, and training activities. It details formal and informal enforcement actions, penalty amounts and disposition, public access to enforcement orders, state member bank reporting requirements, the two-stage appeals process for material supervisory determinations and its 2023 cases, supervision and regulation assessments transferred to the Treasury, and the Federal Reserve’s domestic, international, and minority-bank training and technical-assistance efforts, including 20 foreign-supervisor seminars, approximately 900 participants, and collaboration with the IMF, World Bank, and other partners.

nodes.title: Assessments for Supervision and Regulation
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s MSD appeal process and reports one appeal and one filing extension in 2023; explains supervision and regulation assessments, including their eligible institutions, Treasury transfer, and $771.1 million collected from 53 institutions; and summarizes the Federal Reserve’s training, technical assistance, and outreach activities, including international supervisory programs, 20 seminars attended by about 900 officials, and collaboration with the IMF, World Bank, and other partners.

nodes.title: Training and Technical Assistance
International Training and Technical Assistance
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s MSD appeals process and 2023 appeal activity; supervision and regulation assessments, including eligibility, Treasury treatment, and 2023 collections; training and technical assistance for foreign supervisors; and efforts to support minority-owned depository institutions through the Partnership for Progress. It reports international training activities and partners, explains MDI assistance and portfolio size, highlights two 2023 MDI conferences and forums, and cites relevant statutory and Federal Reserve resources.

nodes.title: Efforts to Support Minority-Owned Depository Institutions
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s 2023 efforts to support minority depository institutions through its Partnership for Progress program, including technical assistance, resources, supervisory guidance, partnerships, and outreach events, while noting its 16-bank MDI portfolio and statutory reporting and preservation duties under Dodd-Frank and FIRREA. It also outlines the Federal Reserve’s international supervisory engagement through the Financial Stability Board, whose 2023 priorities included cross-border payments, crypto-assets and stablecoins, open-ended funds, and third-party risks, and lists related FSB publications. The text additionally explains the purpose and funding of the Emergency Capital Investment Program.

The section reviews Federal Reserve appeals and supervision assessment activities, international training and technical assistance for foreign supervisors, and efforts to support minority-owned depository institutions through the Partnership for Progress, including assistance, outreach, conferences, statutory duties, and the 16-bank MDI portfolio. It also covers international supervisory engagement through the Financial Stability Board and its 2023 priorities and publications, explains the Emergency Capital Investment Program, and cites relevant legal and Federal Reserve resources.

nodes.title: International Engagement
Financial Stability Board
nodes.summary: The text describes Federal Reserve supervisory outreach through PFP initiatives for MDIs and CDFIs, including participation in a National Bankers Association conference, a Bank Term Funding Program webinar, and ECIP technical-assistance efforts. It then reviews the Federal Reserve’s 2023 international engagement through the FSB and BCBS, including objectives related to financial stability, cross-border payments, crypto-assets, open-ended funds, third-party risk, Basel III implementation, banking turmoil, financial digitalization, climate risks, and emerging threats. It lists major FSB and BCBS publications issued during 2023, provides the FSB publication resource, and explains ECIP’s purpose and funding as well as the BCBS’s membership and supervisory role.

nodes.title: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision
nodes.summary: The text reviews the Federal Reserve’s 2023 involvement in international financial-stability, banking-supervision, and payment-infrastructure bodies. It lists major FSB publications on non-bank leverage, cross-border payments, third-party risk, and open-ended-fund liquidity mismatch; describes BCBS priorities and enumerates its final and consultative documents on Basel III, banking turmoil, risk management, climate and crypto disclosures, interest-rate risk, and supervision; and explains CPMI’s work with the FSB and IOSCO to improve cross-border payments, financial-market infrastructures, CCP loss practices, margining, and implementation of infrastructure principles, including a publication on multilateral cross-border-payment platforms.

nodes.title: Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures
nodes.summary: The text reviews 2023 international supervisory and regulatory work involving the BCBS, CPMI, and IAIS. It lists selected BCBS publications and consultations; explains CPMI’s cross-border payments, financial-market-infrastructure, IOSCO, and FSB-related work and identifies its 2023 publications and consultation; and describes the Federal Reserve’s IAIS participation, the IAIS’s progress on insurance capital standards and climate-risk guidance, and a publication on policyholder protection schemes.

nodes.title: International Association of Insurance Supervisors
nodes.summary: The text lists major CPMI publications and one consultative document issued in 2023, with links to the documents and the full CPMI publication catalog. It then describes the Federal Reserve’s participation in IAIS insurance-standard setting, IAIS progress on ICS comparability, ICPs, and climate-risk guidance, and examples of IAIS publications. It explains IPAC’s advisory role and its 2023 work on ICS, life-insurer liquidity, and climate insurance. Finally, it describes the interagency Shared National Credit program, its participating agencies, review schedule, and available information on the 2023 review.

The section surveys the Federal Reserve’s international supervisory and regulatory engagement in 2023 through the FSB, BCBS, CPMI, and IAIS, covering financial stability, banking supervision, Basel III, cross-border payments, financial-market infrastructures, crypto-assets, climate and digital risks, insurance standards, liquidity, and policyholder protection. It identifies major publications and consultations from these bodies, explains related Federal Reserve roles and resources, discusses PFP outreach and ECIP assistance for MDIs and CDFIs, describes IPAC’s insurance-policy work, and concludes with the agencies, schedule, and 2023 information for the Shared National Credit program.

nodes.title: Shared National Credit Program
nodes.summary: The text lists key 2023 IAIS publications and related web resources, then describes the Federal Reserve’s IPAC activities, including advice on international insurance capital standards, its assessment of life-insurer liquidity amid rising rates, and the creation of a climate-focused working group. It also explains the interagency Shared National Credit Program, its participating agencies, review schedule, and links to further information.

nodes.title: Bank Secrecy Act and Anti-Money-Laundering Compliance
nodes.summary: In 2023, the Federal Reserve continued supervising institutions for BSA/AML compliance, helping update the FFIEC examination manual, implementing the AML Act of 2020, and participating in the Treasury-led BSA Advisory Group. It also coordinated internationally on sanctions, money laundering, and counter-terrorism financing, monitored sanctions linked to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, contributed to Financial Action Task Force standards, and supported the Financial Stability Board’s 2023 G20 cross-border payments roadmap progress report.

nodes.title: International Coordination on Sanctions, Anti-Money-Laundering, and Counter-Terrorism Financing
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s 2023 domestic and international efforts on BSA/AML compliance, sanctions, and counter-terrorist financing, including examination-manual revisions, implementation of the AML Act of 2020, participation in advisory, international, and supervisory groups, sanctions monitoring, technical training, and information sharing. It also explains the purpose of Federal Reserve and FFIEC regulatory reports and details the 2023 revisions to the FR Y-7Q report concerning U.S. asset reporting, filing frequency, deadlines, and form clarifications.

The section surveys the Federal Reserve's 2023 supervisory and regulatory work, including risk-based examinations of domestic and foreign banking organizations, five-year supervisory statistics, and the response to the Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank failures. It covers specialized examinations, stress testing and capital planning, operational and cyber resilience, information technology and third-party risks, crypto-asset and dollar-token activities, climate-related financial-risk analysis and principles, enforcement actions and appeals, reporting and supervision assessments, and training and technical assistance. It also reviews support for minority institutions, international engagement through major financial and insurance standard-setting bodies, insurance policy initiatives, the Emergency Capital Investment Program, the Shared National Credit Program, and domestic and international efforts concerning BSA/AML compliance, sanctions, counter-terrorist financing, regulatory reporting, and cross-border payments.

nodes.title: Regulatory Reports
Federal Reserve Regulatory Reports
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s international AML/CFT cooperation and training, its and the FFIEC agencies’ regulatory-reporting requirements, and the purposes of those reports. It details 2023 revisions to Federal Reserve forms FR Y-7Q, FR Y-9C, FR Y-14Q, FR Y-12/Y-12A, and FR 2590, including their purposes and effective dates, as well as FFIEC changes to the Call Reports and FFIEC 002 following statutory review. It concludes by describing the Federal Reserve’s supervisory staff-development program for nearly 4,200 professionals and state-agency staff.

nodes.title: FFIEC Regulatory Reports
nodes.summary: The text describes regulatory-reporting revisions finalized in late 2023, the FFIEC’s uniform reporting requirements and their importance to financial supervision, 2023 changes to the Call Reports and FFIEC 002 following a statutory review, and the Federal Reserve’s supervisory staff development program serving nearly 4,200 professionals and state banking agencies. It also provides the FFIEC reporting-forms website and supporting legal and Federal Register references.

The section covers Federal Reserve and FFIEC regulatory-reporting requirements, their supervisory purposes, international AML/CFT cooperation and training, 2023 revisions to specified Federal Reserve forms and late-2023 changes to the Call Reports and FFIEC 002 following statutory review, along with the Federal Reserve’s supervisory staff-development program, the FFIEC reporting-forms website, and supporting legal and Federal Register references.

nodes.title: Staff Development Programs
nodes.summary: The text describes 2023 changes to Federal Reserve and FFIEC regulatory reporting, including revised Call Reports and FFIEC 002 forms, their effective dates, and the role of uniform reports in supervision and financial-system monitoring. It summarizes Federal Reserve staff-development and FFIEC training programs, including the training categories and statistics presented in table 4.4, explains the three-track examiner commissioning program and its 74 successful examinees, and outlines continuing professional-development resources for Federal Reserve and state supervisory staff.

This section surveys the Federal Reserve’s 2023 supervisory, regulatory, reporting, and staff-development activities. It covers examinations, bank-failure responses, capital and stress supervision, operational, cyber, technology, third-party, crypto, and climate risks, enforcement, minority-institution support, international and insurance initiatives, emergency and shared-credit programs, and AML/CFT and payments work. It also explains Federal Reserve and FFIEC reporting requirements and revisions, including Call Reports and FFIEC 002, related supervisory and legal resources, and examiner training, commissioning, and continuing professional development.

nodes.title: Regulatory Developments
Rulemakings and Guidance
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve's 2023 regulatory and supervisory work, including its methods of issuing rules, statements, letters, and guidance; a chronological catalog of interagency and Federal Reserve actions covering crypto-asset risks, stress testing, Silicon Valley Bank supervision, LIBOR, third-party and liquidity risks, real-estate valuation and lending, capital and resolution requirements, novel activities, CRA, climate risk, consumer rules, payments, and beneficial ownership; and its review of 752 banking applications. It also directs readers to the Federal Reserve's reports, public decision and filing notices, and application guidance.

nodes.title: Banking Applications
nodes.summary: The text lists Federal Reserve and interagency supervision, regulatory, and guidance actions issued from November 13 through December 21, 2023, covering appraisal and consumer-credit thresholds, payment-service pricing, long-term-debt rule comments, reserve requirements, Regulation O and FDIC reporting, Community Reinvestment Act thresholds, and beneficial-ownership information access. It also describes the Federal Reserve's banking-application responsibilities, noting 752 applications acted on in 2023, and identifies its semiannual application-activity reports and online resources for regulatory announcements and application guidance.

nodes.title: Public Notice of Federal Reserve Decisions and Filings Received
nodes.summary: The text records Federal Reserve and interagency regulatory announcements issued in late 2023, covering mortgage appraisal and consumer-credit thresholds, payment-service pricing, long-term-debt rulemaking, reserve requirement indexing, Regulation O and FDIC reporting guidance, and Community Reinvestment Act asset thresholds. It also explains the Federal Reserve’s banking-application review activity, noting 752 actions in 2023, identifies the semiannual applications report, and directs readers to online resources for decisions, announcements, and application guidance.

The section reviews the Federal Reserve’s 2023 regulatory, supervisory, and guidance work, spanning broad financial, banking, consumer, payment, risk-management, capital, resolution, climate, CRA, and beneficial-ownership matters, as well as specific regulatory announcements issued late in the year. It also explains the Federal Reserve’s banking-application review role, noting 752 applications acted on in 2023, and provides references to reports, public notices, regulatory resources, and application guidance.

structure.summary: The section presents the Federal Reserve’s supervision and regulation responsibilities, banking-sector monitoring, and oversight of a broad range of domestic, international, insurance, and financial market institutions. It details institutional conditions and examinations, risk-based supervision, financial market utility and international oversight, supervisory priorities and remediation, and responses to major bank failures. It also reviews 2023 supervisory activities involving capital, stress testing, operational, cyber, technology, third-party, crypto, climate, AML/CFT, payments, enforcement, emergency programs, reporting requirements, examiner development, and support for minority institutions. Finally, it surveys regulatory and guidance initiatives across financial, banking, consumer, payment, risk, capital, resolution, climate, CRA, and beneficial-ownership matters, and explains banking-application reviews and related regulatory resources.

structure.title: 5 Payment System and Reserve Bank Oversight

nodes.title: Payment Services to Depository and Other Institutions
Commercial Check-Collection Service
nodes.summary: The text describes the Reserve Banks' priced payment services and their 2021 organizational restructuring into Federal Reserve Financial Services, prompted partly by changing financial services and the 2023 FedNow® launch. It details the commercial check-collection service, including its offerings, 2023 cost recovery, revenues, expenses, income, processing volumes, declining trends, and outlook, and introduces the commercial ACH service and its domestic, cross-border, same-day, and next-day electronic batch-payment capabilities. It also defines depository institutions and notes their economic and payment-system roles.

nodes.title: Commercial Automated Clearinghouse Service
nodes.summary: The text describes the Reserve Banks' priced payment services and their 2021 consolidation into Federal Reserve Financial Services, including the July 2023 launch of FedNow and goals of greater accessibility, integrity, efficiency, agility, resilience, and customer support. It details the commercial check-collection service, its 2023 financial results and declining processing volumes, explains the ACH service's domestic and cross-border batch-payment capabilities, and defines depository institutions and their economic and payment-system roles.

nodes.title: Box 5.1. Priced Services and Cost Recovery
FedNow Service
nodes.summary: The text presents 2021–23 activity and growth data for Federal Reserve priced services, explains the activity measures and the 2023 expansion of Fedwire Securities pricing to include Treasury securities, and reports 2023 cost recovery, expenses, revenue, income, volumes, and values for commercial ACH, Fedwire Funds, and National Settlement services. It introduces the FedNow instant-payment service launched in July 2023, describing its 24/7 operation, benefits, early adoption by more than 300 institutions, expected growth, and $545 million implementation investment. It also describes the functions and 2023 performance of Fedwire Funds, the National Settlement Service, and the Fedwire Securities Service, with the final description ending mid-sentence.

nodes.title: Fedwire Funds and National Settlement Services
nodes.summary: The text reports Federal Reserve investment in and planned reporting for FedNow, describes the 2023 cost recovery and financial results for Fedwire Funds and National Settlement Services, and explains the purposes and 2023 activity levels of the Fedwire Funds Service and National Settlement Service. It also introduces the Fedwire Securities Service as an electronic depository and real-time settlement system for eligible government-related securities, with its description cut off in the source.

nodes.title: Fedwire Securities Service
nodes.summary: The text reports Federal Reserve investment in and planned reporting for FedNow, 2023 cost recovery and financial results for Fedwire Funds and National Settlement Services, and operational volumes and values for those services. It explains the functions and 2023 performance of Fedwire Funds and the National Settlement Service, then describes Fedwire Securities, including its eligible securities, the 2023 expansion of its priced component to Treasury securities, financial results, transfer activity, payment flows, and securities held and outstanding. It concludes by describing the six FedLine Solutions used to access Reserve Bank services, their fee and cost allocation structure, customer requirements, and the 2023 migration toward newer connectivity options.

nodes.title: FedLine Solutions: Access to Reserve Bank Services
nodes.summary: The text reports 2023 activity and financial performance for the Fedwire Securities Service, including its securities-transfer, payment, and depository functions, with Treasury transfers newly added to the priced component and causing a large reported increase in volume. It also describes FedLine Solutions as the Reserve Banks’ six access options for priced services and the migration away from legacy products. Finally, it explains Federal Reserve intraday credit and daylight overdrafts, their benefits, governance, declining use and fees due to high overnight balances, ample reserves, and the elimination of fees for collateralized overdrafts.

nodes.title: Federal Reserve Intraday Credit
nodes.summary: The text discusses legacy payment-product pricing and discontinuation, then explains Federal Reserve oversight of intraday credit or daylight overdrafts, which occur when an institution's account temporarily becomes negative during the day. These overdrafts facilitate payments and reduce risk, but their use and associated fees have stayed low from 2007 through 2023 because institutions hold large overnight balances. The 2011 elimination of fees for collateralized overdrafts contributed further to lower fee revenue. Federal Reserve policy provides no-cost collateralized intraday credit to healthy institutions, and usage is expected to remain low under the ample-reserves monetary-policy regime.

This section explains the Federal Reserve's requirement to recover the full direct, indirect, and imputed costs of its priced payment and settlement services, including the PSAF, and presents 2014–23 cost-recovery results and accounting adjustments. It reports the 2023 financial and operational performance of commercial ACH, Fedwire Funds, National Settlement, and Fedwire Securities, including the expansion of priced Treasury-security transfers. It introduces the July 2023 FedNow instant-payment service, its continuous operation, early adoption, implementation investment, expected growth, and delayed cost-recovery expectations. The section also describes FedLine access products and their migration from legacy systems, and discusses intraday credit and daylight overdrafts, their payment and risk-management benefits, oversight and collateral policies, and declining use and fees under ample reserves.

The section reviews the Reserve Banks’ priced payment services and their consolidation into Federal Reserve Financial Services, covering commercial check collection and ACH services, their capabilities, financial results, cost recovery, and declining check volumes. It explains depository institutions’ roles and the requirement to recover the full costs of priced services, with 2014–23 results and 2023 performance for ACH, Fedwire Funds, National Settlement, and Fedwire Securities. It also covers the July 2023 launch and development of FedNow, FedLine access products and modernization, and intraday credit and daylight overdrafts, including their benefits, safeguards, and declining use and fees.

nodes.title: Currency and Coin
Banknote Development
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s currency and coin distribution responsibilities, 2023 note and coin circulation volumes, changes in net note payments and currency outstanding, and initiatives to modernize U.S. currency and develop its next banknote family. It also explains the roles of the Board, Reserve Banks, U.S. Mint, Treasury, Bureau of Engraving and Printing, Federal Reserve Financial Services, and Secret Service in currency issuance, security, design, and technology development.

nodes.title: Box 5.2. U.S. Currency Program Initiatives
nodes.summary: The text describes Federal Reserve and BEP efforts to modernize and secure the U.S. Currency Program through new processing equipment, possible regionalization, upgraded Reserve Bank and BEP facilities, and development of a new banknote family beginning with the $10 note planned for 2026. It covers security-feature research and adversarial counterfeit analysis, the CEP’s education and outreach activities and 2023 results, and the Board’s cooperation with domestic and international central-bank and cash-machine groups to preserve confidence in U.S. currency. It also notes the essential nature of currency issuance, the dollar’s global reserve-currency role, and the Board’s obligation to reimburse BEP for production costs.

The section explains how the Federal Reserve and partner agencies issue, distribute, secure, and modernize U.S. currency and coin. It reviews 2023 circulation and currency-outstanding trends; institutional responsibilities; efforts involving processing equipment, facilities, possible regionalization, security research, counterfeit analysis, public education, and development of a new banknote family starting with a planned 2026 $10 note; cooperation with domestic and international organizations; and the importance of reliable currency issuance, the dollar’s reserve-currency role, and reimbursement of banknote production costs.

nodes.title: Fiscal Agency and Government Depository Services
Payment Services
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve Banks’ role as fiscal agents and depositories for the Treasury and other entities, including their payment, financing and securities, accounting, reporting, technology, and cash-management services. It reports 2023 reimbursable expenses of $770.4 million, their allocation and decline from prior years, and details Treasury payment operations such as federal disbursements, collections, Stored Value Cards, Pay.gov, and related transaction volumes. It also explains Reserve Bank support for Treasury borrowing and securities administration, noting 428 auctions and $22.0 trillion in securities awarded in 2023.

nodes.title: Financing and Securities Services
nodes.summary: The text describes Reserve Bank services supporting the Treasury’s payment operations, financing and securities activities, accounting and reporting, and technology infrastructure. It reports 2023 service expenses, changes and their causes, details Stored Value Card and Pay.gov operations and transaction volumes, summarizes Treasury securities auctions and servicing, explains accounting systems and federal financial publications, and notes infrastructure, demand, accounting-method, and publication-reference details.

nodes.title: Accounting and Reporting Services
nodes.summary: The text describes Reserve Bank support for Treasury securities, accounting, reporting, and technology services. It reports 2023 service volumes and expenses, including $427.5 billion in savings bonds and marketable securities, $194.4 million in financing and securities expenses after a Fedwire accounting change, and $81.1 million in accounting and reporting expenses driven higher by technical-debt remediation, cybersecurity, and cloud migration. It explains the functions of the Cash Accounting Reporting System and G-Invoicing, outlines the Treasury reports supported by the Reserve Banks, describes their infrastructure and technology responsibilities, and notes a 164 percent increase in Treasury product demand due largely to higher marketable-security interest rates.

nodes.title: Infrastructure and Technology Services
nodes.summary: The text describes Reserve Bank support for Treasury securities, accounting and reporting, technology infrastructure, and banking services for other entities, including 2023 expenses and the reasons for their changes. It explains key systems such as the Cash Accounting Reporting System and G-Invoicing, ongoing cloud migration, automation, lifecycle planning, and cybersecurity efforts, as well as related Treasury publications and the Cloud Smart strategy. It also outlines the Federal Reserve’s broader payment-system roles as operator, supervisor, regulator, researcher, and catalyst for improvements, including research into payment, clearing, settlement, and financial-market infrastructures.

nodes.title: Services Provided to Other Entities
nodes.summary: In 2023, the Reserve Banks advanced cloud migration, automation, infrastructure management, and cybersecurity, reducing infrastructure and technology expenses to $143.6 million. They also provided authorized U.S.-dollar banking and electronic securities services to other entities, including Ginnie Mae, with related expenses falling to $14.9 million. The Federal Reserve additionally serves as a payment-system operator, supervisor and regulator, researcher, and catalyst for improvements, conducting research on payment, clearing, settlement, and financial market infrastructures and their role in economic activity. The text also references the federal Cloud Smart strategy.

The section explains how the Federal Reserve Banks support the Treasury and other authorized entities as fiscal agents, depositories, payment operators, and providers of financing and securities, accounting and reporting, technology, cash-management, and banking services. It covers 2023 expenses and service volumes, Treasury disbursements and collections, Stored Value Cards and Pay.gov, securities auctions and servicing, accounting systems and federal reporting, and services for entities such as Ginnie Mae. It also describes cloud migration, automation, cybersecurity, infrastructure planning, demand and accounting changes, and the Federal Reserve’s broader supervisory, regulatory, research, and catalytic roles in improving payment, clearing, settlement, and financial-market infrastructures.

nodes.title: Evolutions and Improvements to the System
Payment System Research and Analysis
nodes.summary: The text describes the Reserve Banks’ 2023 technology and service activities, including cloud migration, infrastructure modernization, cybersecurity, and related expense declines. It details dollar-denominated banking, securities, and safekeeping services provided to other entities and the associated reduction in expenses. It then outlines the Federal Reserve’s broader payment-system roles as operator, regulator, supervisor, researcher, and improvement catalyst; summarizes research on payment methods, innovation, infrastructures, and fraud; discusses digital-innovation research involving digital assets, CBDCs, cross-border and wholesale payments, and related risks; highlights international and domestic collaboration; and explains the Board’s statutory responsibility to regulate payment and settlement activities.

nodes.title: Digital Innovations Research
nodes.summary: The text outlines Federal Reserve research and oversight of payment systems. It summarizes 2023 research on payment-method trends, innovations such as instant payments and digital assets, financial-market infrastructures, and fraud; describes research into digital assets, CBDCs, emerging technologies, cross-border and wholesale payments, and related policy and infrastructure implications; notes extensive international and domestic collaboration; and explains the Board’s congressional responsibility to implement payment- and banking-related laws through regulation, with links to relevant Federal Reserve resources.

nodes.title: Payment System Regulation
nodes.summary: The text reviews Federal Reserve oversight, research, regulation, and modernization of payment systems. It covers 2023 research on payment trends, innovation, infrastructure, and fraud; digital-asset and payment-technology research and related domestic and international collaboration; Regulation II debit-card interchange-fee revisions; creation of a public database for Reserve Bank master-account and service access; implementation of FedNow; modernization, resilience, cybersecurity, and FedLine improvements; replacement of currency-processing equipment; and the refreshed 2024–26 System IT Strategic Plan.

nodes.title: Other Improvements and Efforts
nodes.summary: The text covers proposed Regulation II debit-interchange-fee changes and biennial updates, creation of the public Master Account and Services Database, and Reserve Bank efforts involving FedNow, payment-platform modernization, currency-processing equipment, IT strategy and datacenter modernization, cybersecurity, and facility upgrades. It points to table G.13 for facility asset information and describes Reserve Bank oversight through independent annual audits, Board reviews, and use of the 2013 COSO internal-control framework.

The section describes Reserve Bank and Federal Reserve efforts to improve payment systems through technology modernization, cloud and datacenter upgrades, FedNow and FedLine enhancements, cybersecurity, resilience, currency-processing equipment replacement, facility improvements, and the 2024–26 System IT Strategic Plan. It covers banking, securities, and safekeeping services and related expense reductions; the Federal Reserve’s operational, regulatory, supervisory, research, and improvement roles; research on payment trends, fraud, infrastructures, instant payments, digital assets, CBDCs, emerging technologies, and cross-border and wholesale payments; and domestic and international collaboration. It also addresses statutory payment-system regulation, Regulation II interchange-fee changes, the public Master Account and Services Database, facility assets, and oversight through audits, Board reviews, and COSO-based internal controls.

nodes.title: Oversight of Federal Reserve Banks
Income and Expenses
nodes.summary: The text describes annual Board and external oversight of SOMA and foreign-currency operations, including compliance, technology, resiliency, and auditing reviews, and presents the Reserve Banks’ 2023 financial results and distribution framework. Income rose modestly, while expenses surged, producing a large net loss and causing most Banks to suspend Treasury remittances and record deferred assets, though $670 million was transferred in 2023. The accompanying table details major income, expense, loss, assessment, consolidated-entity, dividend, remittance, deferred-asset, and comprehensive-income categories for 2023 and 2022, while Appendix G supplies extensive financial, budgetary, and employment statistics.

nodes.title: SOMA Holdings
nodes.summary: The text describes SOMA's role in holding securities acquired through FOMC-directed open market operations, identifies the types of assets held, references a table comparing SOMA financial metrics for 2023 and 2022, reports 2023 balances and interest rates for major Reserve Bank lending programs, and explains pandemic-related SPV lending and liquidity support, with a cross-reference to appendix G for Treasury and agency-security holdings.

nodes.title: Lending
nodes.summary: The text describes the FOMC-directed SOMA operations of the New York Fed, identifies the securities and investments held, presents 2023 versus 2022 SOMA asset, liability, income, expense, interest-rate, and net-holding data, and explains the principal changes in those balances. It also reports average lending balances and rates for Reserve Bank credit programs, describes pandemic-related SPV lending, and defines the table's valuation, accounting, and notation footnotes.

The section covers Reserve Bank payment-system modernization, cybersecurity, facility improvements, financial reporting, and comprehensive Board and independent-auditor oversight. It explains COSO-based internal-control assessments, KPMG’s 2023 audits and independence requirements, ongoing risk and internal-audit reviews, and the oversight of SOMA and foreign-currency operations. It also summarizes 2023 financial results and remittances, deferred assets, SOMA holdings and year-over-year financial changes, Reserve Bank lending programs, pandemic-related lending vehicles, and related tables, accounting notes, and appendix references.

nodes.title: Pro Forma Financial Statements for Federal Reserve Priced Services
Notes to Pro Forma Financial Statements for Priced Services
(1) Short-Term Assets
nodes.summary: The notes explain the composition and treatment of short- and long-term priced-service assets, including receivables, collection items, float costs, shared assets, deferred taxes, and Board assets. They describe the matched-book financing and imputed equity structure, provide 2023 and 2022 capitalization percentages and the 2022 revision, and introduce the Board's Payment System Risk policy and its basis in international financial market infrastructure standards and expectations for Fedwire Services.

nodes.title: (2) Long-Term Assets
nodes.summary: The notes explain the composition and treatment of short- and long-term priced-service assets, including receivables, collection items, float costs, shared assets, deferred taxes, and Board assets. They describe the matched-book financing and imputed-equity structure, provide 2023 and 2022 capitalization percentages and the 2022 revision, and introduce the Board's Payment System Risk policy and its international standards basis for Fedwire Services.

nodes.title: (3) Liabilities and Equity
nodes.summary: The notes explain the composition and accounting treatment of priced-service assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, and operating expenses. They describe collection float and its valuation, long-term assets and deferred taxes, matched-book financing and FDIC-based imputed equity levels, Payment System Risk liquidity requirements, and pension and postretirement benefit accounting under ASC 715. They also report related 2022–2023 balances, expenses, restatements, and changes in accumulated other comprehensive loss, identify priced-service revenue and expense categories, disclose Board and pension costs, exclude FedNow development expenses, and note the 2019 pension-cost disaggregation update whose explanation is truncated.

nodes.title: (4) Revenue
nodes.summary: The text explains Fedwire Funds risk-management and capital-support requirements, including the maintenance of six months of operating expenses in liquid assets and equity and the absence of needed imputed balances in 2023 and 2022. It describes ASC 715 treatment of pension and other benefit plans, related pension assets, liabilities, deferred taxes, and AOCI changes. It then defines priced-service revenue and operating expenses, identifies covered services and Board costs, excludes FedNow development expenses, reports qualified and nonqualified pension service costs, and notes the ASC 715 disaggregation requirement and restatement of the prior-year pension asset.

nodes.title: (5) Operating Expenses
nodes.summary: The text explains Reserve Bank oversight and accounting for priced payment services, including Fedwire Funds capital and liquidity requirements, pension-plan recognition under ASC 715, revenue and operating-expense composition, pension service costs, AOCI treatment, and service-level income-statement components. It details the PSAF-based methodology for imputed taxes, equity returns, debt interest, sales taxes, and float, explains allocation and actual-float recovery, and reports 2023 and 2022 expense, pension, tax-rate, and float amounts, including relevant restatements and definitions.

nodes.title: (6) Imputed Costs
nodes.summary: The text explains Reserve Bank service accounting, including ASC 715 benefit-plan treatment, service-level income-statement categories and tax rates, PSAF-based imputed costs and their allocation, the calculation and recovery of credit float, and related footnote definitions. It also describes imputed investment income and defines annual cost recovery as total revenue including other income relative to operating expenses, imputed costs and taxes, and the targeted after-tax return on equity.

nodes.title: (7) Other Income and Expenses
nodes.summary:
Payment System and Reserve Bank Oversight 81
Float that is created by account adjustments due to transaction errors and the observance of non- standard holidays by some depository institutions was recovered from the depository institutions through charging institutions directly. Float subject to recovery is valued at the federal funds rate. Certain ACH funding requirements and check products generate credit float; this float has been subtracted from the cost base subject to recovery in 2023 and 2022.

Other income consists of income on imputed investments. Excess financing resulting from addi- tional equity imputed to meet the FDIC well-capitalized requirements is assumed to be invested and earning interest at the 3-month Treasury bill rate.

Annual cost recovery is the ratio of revenue, including other income, to the sum of operating expenses, imputed costs, imputed income taxes, and after-tax targeted return on equity.
