The section explains the financial-statement accounting and cost-recovery framework for priced services. It covers short- and long-term assets, liabilities, equity, matched-book financing, imputed capitalization, Payment System Risk liquidity requirements, float valuation and recovery, deferred taxes, pension and postretirement benefits under ASC 715, revenue and operating-expense categories, Board and pension costs, and the exclusion of FedNow development expenses. It also details PSAF-based imputed taxes, financing costs, equity returns, sales taxes, and float allocations; reports related 2022–2023 balances, expenses, tax rates, restatements, and accumulated other comprehensive loss changes; describes income from imputed investments; and defines annual cost recovery as revenue and other income relative to operating expenses, imputed costs and taxes, and the targeted after-tax return on equity.

This section presents the 2023 and 2022 pro forma balance sheets and income statements for Federal Reserve priced services, including asset, liability, equity, revenue, expense, imputed-cost, tax, net-income, and targeted-return information. It also provides a 2023 service-level breakdown for commercial check collection, ACH, Fedwire Funds, and Fedwire Securities, with cost-recovery results and an exclusion for FedNow development expenses. The accompanying notes explain the accounting, financing, capitalization, float, tax, pension, benefit, revenue, expense, and cost-recovery methods used, along with related restatements, comparative balances, and accumulated other comprehensive loss.

structure.summary: The section reviews how the Federal Reserve maintains the reliability, security, and integrity of the U.S. payment and settlement system. It covers priced payment services and their financial and operational performance, the launch and expansion of FedNow, FedLine and intraday-credit services, currency and coin distribution and modernization, and fiscal-agent, depository, payment, securities, accounting, technology, and cash-management services for the Treasury and other entities. It also describes payment-system modernization, cybersecurity, resilience, infrastructure improvements, research and collaboration on emerging and cross-border payment technologies, regulatory and catalytic activities, and comprehensive Reserve Bank oversight through internal controls, audits, risk reviews, and Board supervision. Finally, it presents Reserve Bank financial results, SOMA and lending operations, and pro forma financial statements and accounting notes for priced services, including service-level cost recovery and related assumptions.

structure.title: 6 Consumer and Community Affairs

nodes.title: Consumer Compliance Supervision
Consumer Compliance Examinations
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s consumer and community affairs responsibilities, including oversight of examiner training and resources, application analysis, and consumer complaints. It explains that consumer compliance examinations are the main supervisory tool, reports 2023 examination activity and updated HMDA guidance, and outlines the Federal Reserve’s and CFPB’s respective authorities. It details CRA responsibilities, 2023 CRA examination ratings, and the agencies’ October 2023 final CRA modernization rule. Finally, it introduces fair-lending and UDAP enforcement under ECOA, the Fair Housing Act, and the FTC Act, including ECOA’s prohibited bases of credit discrimination and protections for public-assistance recipients and consumers exercising legal rights.

nodes.title: Consumer Compliance Enforcement Activities
Fair Lending and UDAP Enforcement
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s 2023 community reinvestment, consumer compliance, fair lending, UDAP, and flood insurance activities. It explains the CRA mandate and the Federal Reserve’s examination, application-review, and community-development roles; reports 174 CRA examinations with 23 Outstanding and 151 Satisfactory ratings; and notes the agencies’ October 2023 CRA final rule. It outlines ECOA, FHA, and FTC Act protections, supervisory authority divided between the Federal Reserve and CFPB, definitions of unfair and deceptive practices, specialized review and DOJ referral procedures, and enforcement tools. In 2023, one marital-status discrimination matter was referred to the DOJ, while extensive outreach included a 6,300-plus-person webinar and compliance publications. The text also explains flood insurance requirements for loans in special flood hazard areas and reports a 2023 enforcement order imposing approximately $2.9455 million in penalties, allocated between FEMA and the Treasury.

nodes.title: Flood Insurance Enforcement
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve's use of informal and public enforcement tools, its outreach and transparency efforts on fair lending and unfair or deceptive acts or practices, the 2023 fair lending webinar and compliance publication, and the legal requirements for flood insurance on certain loans. It reports a 2023 flood insurance enforcement action totaling approximately $2.9455 million, with penalties distributed between FEMA's National Flood Mitigation Fund and the U.S. Treasury, and includes related informational links.

The section reviews the Federal Reserve’s 2023 CRA, consumer compliance, fair lending, UDAP, and flood insurance supervision and enforcement. It covers CRA examinations and ratings, the 2023 CRA final rule, applicable fair lending and consumer protection laws, agency responsibilities and enforcement procedures, a DOJ referral for marital-status discrimination, outreach and compliance resources, flood insurance requirements, and a major flood insurance enforcement action imposing approximately $2.9455 million in penalties.

nodes.title: Mergers and Acquisitions
nodes.summary: The text explains the legal and supervisory factors the Federal Reserve considers in merger and acquisition applications, including competition, financial condition, management and compliance, CRA performance, community needs, and stability. It describes the compliance, supervisory, examiner, applicant, and public information used in reviews, possible pre-membership examinations, and the Board's publication of transaction Orders and semiannual application statistics and processing analyses. It also covers 2023 coordination with the CFPB and other regulators under an interagency agreement designed to promote cooperation, share examination schedules, and reduce regulatory duplication and burden, with footnotes directing readers to related guidance and Federal Reserve resources.

nodes.title: Coordination with Other Agencies
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve Board's legal and supervisory review of mergers and acquisitions, including competitive, financial, managerial, compliance, CRA, community, and stability considerations. It explains the information reviewed, possible pre-membership examinations, public disclosure through Orders and press releases, and semiannual reporting on application outcomes, processing times, withdrawals, and public comments. It also covers 2023 supervisory coordination with the CFPB and other regulators under an interagency agreement intended to reduce burden, duplication, and conflicting directives through cooperation and shared examination planning, and references related guidance and reports.

nodes.title: Box 6.1. Supporting Consumer Protection and Community Development
Modernizing the Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
nodes.summary: Box 6.1 describes the Federal Reserve’s 2023 consumer-protection and community-development work amid post-pandemic changes, inflation, and evolving banking technology. Through DCCA, the Board advanced financial-inclusion policy, modernized CRA regulations with the FDIC and OCC, promoted fair lending and consumer-compliance risk management, highlighted discrimination and algorithmic-bias concerns, and reported on common legal violations and mitigation practices. It also researched household financial well-being through the 2022 SHED survey and shared findings on emergency costs, employment, inflation, education, housing, and retirement savings through a public webinar, with accompanying online resources.

nodes.title: Promoting Sound Consumer Risk-Management Practices among Banks
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s 2023 efforts to support consumer protection, financial inclusion, and community development amid the end of pandemic assistance, inflation, and technological change in banking. It highlights DCCA guidance, research, and outreach; the interagency modernization of CRA rules to reflect digital banking and differing bank models while supporting low- and moderate-income communities; fair-lending and consumer-compliance risk-management initiatives addressing discrimination, algorithmic bias, redlining, and appraisal issues; and research from the 2022 household economic well-being survey on financial pressures, employment, inflation, education, housing, and retirement. It also references related online resources.

nodes.title: Conducting Research and Analysis of Emerging Consumer Issues
nodes.summary: The text reviews the Federal Reserve’s 2023 consumer-protection and community-development work amid post-pandemic policy changes, inflation, and banking innovation. It describes DCCA’s regulatory, research, and outreach efforts; the interagency modernization of CRA rules to improve fair and effective credit access, especially in low- and moderate-income communities; initiatives promoting fair lending and consumer-law compliance; and research on household economic well-being through the SHED survey and related outreach. It also references supporting online resources.

nodes.title: Box 6.1—continued
nodes.summary: The text describes Federal Reserve consumer and community affairs research, outreach, and supervisory coordination. It covers publications on small-dollar lending, auto finance, workers’ finances, student debt, SNAP benefit reductions, pandemic earnings, and women’s workforce participation; engagement with communities and stakeholders on post-pandemic economic conditions, credit access, and housing; advisory input from the Community Advisory Council; a Fed Listens event; and a housing-focused research seminar series. It also explains supervisory cooperation through simultaneous exams, report review, information sharing, interagency guidance, FFIEC examination standardization, and participation in the Joint Task Force on Fair Lending, with supporting footnote links.

nodes.title: Engaging with Consumer and Community Perspectives
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s 2023 consumer and community affairs work, including research and publications on credit products, consumer financial well-being, debt, hardship, income, and workforce participation; outreach on post-pandemic economic, housing, credit, and low- and moderate-income community conditions; and housing-focused research seminars. It also covers coordination with federal banking and other agencies through examinations, guidance, fair-lending and appraisal initiatives, HMDA and LIBOR-related interagency statements, and modernization of CRA regulations. Finally, it summarizes public outreach publications and webinars and the Examiner Training program for consumer-compliance supervisory staff.

nodes.title: Outreach
nodes.summary: The text covers Federal Reserve interagency work addressing appraisal bias, 2023 guidance on HMDA reporting following a court decision, the transition away from USD LIBOR, and modernization of CRA regulations. It also describes the Federal Reserve’s outreach activities, including compliance publications and a fair-lending webinar, and introduces its examiner training program for developing consumer compliance supervisory expertise.

nodes.title: Examiner Training
nodes.summary: The text describes 2023 Federal Reserve interagency regulatory actions concerning appraisal bias, HMDA reporting relief, LIBOR transition, and CRA modernization. It then covers the System’s outreach activities, including Consumer Compliance Outlook publications and a fair-lending webinar; examiner education through commissioning, proficiency testing, and continuing professional development; and rapid-response training on emerging supervisory issues. Finally, it explains the Federal Reserve’s role in investigating complaints against its regulated entities and referring other complaints to the appropriate authorities.

nodes.title: Responding to Consumer Complaints and Inquiries
Consumer Complaints
nodes.summary: The text reports 2023 consumer complaint patterns, processing activity, contact methods, resolution outcomes, discrimination allegations, and investigative findings for Federal Reserve-regulated entities. It also describes the Board's consumer-law and fair-lending responsibilities and announces inflation-indexed 2024 increases to Regulation Z/M transaction exemptions and the appraisal exemption threshold for small higher-priced mortgage loans.

Model Validation Council
The Model Validation Council was established in 2012 by the Board of Governors to provide expert and independent advice on its process to rigorously assess the models used in stress tests of banking institutions. The Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act required the Federal Reserve to conduct annual stress tests of large bank holding companies and systemically important, nonbank financial institutions supervised by the Board. The Model Validation Council provides input on the Board’s efforts to assess the effectiveness of the models used in the stress tests. The council is intended to improve the quality of the Federal Reserve’s model assessment program and to strengthen the confidence in the integrity and independence of the program.

nodes.summary: The text reports the Federal Reserve Board’s 2023 actual and budgeted operating expenses, 2024 operating budget, account-level spending, OIG finances, authorized staffing, and capital budgets. Board operations cost $994.1 million in 2023 against a $989.6 million budget and are budgeted at $1,044.1 million in 2024, while OIG operations totaled $34.6 million in 2023 and are budgeted at $39.0 million in 2024. Expenses are detailed by division and by personnel, goods-and-services, overhead, depreciation, and revenue classifications. The 2024 budget supports compensation, critical hiring, strategic contractors, and ongoing services, with new initiatives offset by existing savings. Authorized Board positions rise by 17 to 3,007, and 2024 capital plans include $25.1 million in single-year projects and $364.3 million in multiyear building improvements.

nodes.title: 2024 Capital Budgets
nodes.summary: The text presents a staffing table for Board of Governors divisions, offices, and special accounts, showing 2023 budgeted and actual authorized positions, variances, and 2024 budgets, with totals of 2,990 Board operations positions in 2023 and 3,007 planned for 2024, plus separate figures for the Inspector General and Currency functions. It defines budget and actual counts and the extraordinary-items pool. It also explains the 2024 single-year and multiyear capital budgets, including their amounts, increases, deferred purchases, routine replacements, building projects, and goals of improving workplace security, modernization, collaboration, efficiency, productivity, and sustainability.

nodes.title: Office of Inspector General
nodes.summary: The text explains the OIG’s strategically grounded and statutorily independent budgeting process, reports 2023 operating and capital budget performance—including CFPB-related income and pandemic-response workload changes—and presents the 2024 operating and capital budgets, their year-over-year changes, underlying drivers, and planned capital uses, with references to supporting tables and the strategic plan.

nodes.title: 2023 Budget Performance
nodes.summary: The text explains that the OIG independently prepares its budget according to strategic-plan goals and submits it directly to the Board. It reports 2023 operating and capital budget performance, including expenses, operating income, CFPB-related work, and COVID-19 oversight changes, then outlines the 2024 operating and capital budgets, their year-over-year changes and drivers, planned capital projects, and the tables documenting these figures.

nodes.title: 2024 Operating Expense Budget
nodes.summary: The text explains the OIG’s strategically grounded and statutorily independent budgeting process, reports its 2023 operating and capital budget performance—including CFPB-related income and work—and presents the 2024 operating and capital budgets, their increases and underlying drivers, planned capital uses, and referenced budget tables and strategic-plan link.

nodes.title: 2024 Capital Budget
nodes.summary: The text explains the OIG’s independent, strategic-plan-based budgeting, presents its 2023 operating and capital performance, details its 2024 operating and capital budgets and staffing, and summarizes Board and OIG capital expenditure figures and variances for 2023–24. It then introduces Federal Reserve Bank budgeting, including their strategic alignment, major functional responsibilities, and a budget-process restructuring into five umbrella committees.

The section covers the Board of Governors’ and OIG’s operating, staffing, and capital budgets, including budget preparation, strategic and statutory oversight, approval, monitoring, reporting, and detailed 2023 performance and 2024 plans. It presents Board and OIG expenses, revenues, capital projects, staffing levels, organizational and accounting changes, budget variances, and the priorities and drivers behind new spending, while describing capital investments in facilities, security, modernization, efficiency, and sustainability. It also introduces Federal Reserve Bank budgeting, its functional responsibilities, strategic alignment, and committee-based process restructuring.

nodes.title: Federal Reserve Banks Budgets
2023 Budget Performance
nodes.summary: The text presents 2023 budget, actual, and 2024 budget operating expenses for the Federal Reserve Banks by account classification. Total 2023 actual expenses were $5.6483 billion, just $2.1 million above budget, while the approved 2024 budget was $6.0532 billion, 7.2 percent higher. It details category-level amounts and variances, explains the main causes of 2023 overruns and offsets, reports staffing and capital expenditure underspending, describes drivers of the 2024 increases in monetary policy and Treasury expenses, defines the accounting categories through footnotes, and records the Board’s approval of the 2024 budget.

nodes.title: 2024 Operating Expense Budget
nodes.summary: The excerpt presents Federal Reserve Bank operating-expense, employment, and capital-budget data for 2023–24, including account-level and District-level tables, budget-to-actual variances, staffing totals, and explanatory notes. It describes the near-budget 2023 operating results, the higher 2024 operating and personnel budgets, staffing growth, the drivers of spending increases, major 2024 capital investments, and projects requiring conditional approval.

nodes.title: 2024 Capital Budgets
nodes.summary: The text presents Reserve Bank and National IT capital-expenditure budgets, actual 2023 spending, variances, and 2024 budgets by District, with combined totals of $645.5 million in 2023 actual expenditures and $913.8 million budgeted for 2024. It describes related salary and variable-pay programs, the purposes of 2024 capital investments, conditionally approved and other capital projects, and small capital initiatives. It also explains the currency budget's support for Federal Reserve note production, distribution, quality, security, and issuance strategy, along with the Board's statutory reimbursement obligations to the BEP and the criteria and process for conditional capital approval.

This section reviews Federal Reserve System budgeting, beginning with Board and OIG capital expenditures and staffing, then detailing how the 12 Reserve Banks establish, coordinate, review, approve, and monitor operating and capital budgets. It reports 2023 actual, budgeted, and 2024 projected Reserve Bank expenses by District, operating area, and account classification, along with employment and capital data, variances, accounting definitions, and exclusions. It explains near-budget 2023 results, the higher 2024 operating and personnel budgets and their drivers, salary and variable-pay programs, and Board approval. It also covers Reserve Bank and National IT capital spending, major and conditional projects, small initiatives, currency operations and note-production support, and statutory reimbursements to the Bureau of Engraving and Printing.

nodes.title: Currency Budget
2023 Budget Performance
nodes.summary: The text explains the Federal Reserve's currency-program responsibilities, including note quality control, anti-counterfeiting work, banknote development, and public and institutional currency education. It outlines the annual budget process involving RBOPS, the BEP, Board staff, BAC, and the Board; reports that 2023 BEP and Board operating costs came in below budget, including the effect of a $24.2 million reimbursement credit; and presents the 2024 single-cycle budget of $1.104 billion, with detailed BEP printing/support and Board issuance, development, and education allocations, along with reimbursement true-up and cost-category notes.

nodes.title: 2024 Budget
BEP Single-Cycle Operating Costs
nodes.summary: The text explains the composition of the BEP operating budget, presents the 2023–24 funding and spending figures for three major multicycle capital projects—including their approval history—and details the proposed 2024 single-cycle printing and support budget, separating fixed and variable costs and explaining the reasons for their increases.

nodes.title: BEP Multicycle Project Operating Costs
nodes.summary: The text explains the Federal Reserve's 2024 currency budget, separating BEP single-cycle operating costs, multicycle capital projects, and Board costs. It provides detailed 2023–24 budgets and lifetime funding for the Fort Worth expansion, Washington, D.C., replacement facility, and note-production equipment; describes approved and conditional funding; and outlines the 2024 allocations. It reports increases in fixed and variable BEP printing costs and explains their drivers, presents the scope of a historical currency-cost figure, and details the Board's increased currency-issuance and banknote-development expenses, including strategic initiatives, transportation, security testing, usability, and design programs.

nodes.title: Board Single-Cycle Operating Costs
nodes.summary: The text details Federal Reserve currency-related multicycle and single-cycle budgets. It reports $2,853.9 million in approved multicycle funding for WCF and DCRF facilities and BEP note-production equipment, plus $478.0 million in conditional equipment funding and a $1,265.0 million lifetime equipment-replacement plan through 2033. It explains the 2014–2024 cost figure and its revised treatment of multicycle projects, lists 2024 project allocations, and describes the $70.2 million Board operating budget and its 7.6 percent increase. It identifies drivers of higher issuance and banknote-development costs, outlines currency-education priorities, notes two added positions, and specifies included personnel, operating, and enterprise-support overhead costs.

The section presents the Federal Reserve’s 2024 currency budget, covering BEP single-cycle printing and support costs, major multicycle facility and equipment projects, and Board operating expenses. It compares 2023 budgets with actual spending, explains variances and reimbursement adjustments, details 2024 allocations and lifetime project funding—including approved, conditional, and planned equipment investments—and describes the operational, personnel, transportation, security, development, education, and design initiatives driving the budgets.

The section describes Federal Reserve capital spending and the currency budget, including infrastructure and technology investments, BEP reimbursement and note-production costs, currency transportation and program management, and the Board’s responsibilities for banknote supply, quality, security, design, and education. It reviews the 2023 budget process and below-budget performance, including reimbursement adjustments, and presents the $1.104 billion 2024 single-cycle budget with BEP, Board, operational, development, education, transportation, security, and multiyear facility and equipment allocations, while explaining project approval categories, spending variances, statutory reimbursement requirements, and the annual BEP print-order process.

structure.summary: This section presents the Federal Reserve System’s 2023 budgeting results and 2024 operating and capital plans for the Board of Governors, OIG, Reserve Banks, and currency program. It explains budgeting, strategic alignment, statutory oversight, approval, monitoring, reporting, accounting, organizational changes, and key spending and staffing drivers. It covers expenses, revenues, reimbursements, employment, variances, capital projects, technology and payment modernization, supervision, facilities, security, efficiency, sustainability, National IT, and Reserve Bank operations. It also details currency infrastructure, banknote production and transportation, BEP reimbursements, and the 2023 and 2024 currency budgets, including project categories, allocations, approval requirements, and annual print-order procedures.

structure.title: E Record of Policy Actions of the Board of Governors

nodes.title: Rules and Regulations
Regulation BB (Community Reinvestment)
nodes.summary: The excerpt summarizes two Board rulemakings. The modernized CRA Regulation BB rule, jointly issued with the FDIC and OCC and effective April 1, 2024 with some delayed provisions, introduces tiered, metrics-based evaluations, broader geographic coverage, and clearer community development standards; a March 2024 joint rule extended certain dates and made technical amendments. The CRA action passed with Governor Bowman dissenting. A separate rule, effective April 1, 2024 and jointly issued with the FDIC, OCC, and NCUA, updates administrative practice rules to support electronic communications and more efficient, fair adjudications, while also revising Board-specific procedures; it received unanimous support from the listed governors.

nodes.title: Rules of Practice and Procedure
nodes.summary: The text records 2023-2024 Federal Reserve actions on Community Reinvestment Act regulations, administrative practice and procedure, credit-loss allowances, commercial real estate loan accommodations and workouts, and Section 9(13) activity restrictions. It gives effective dates, joint-agency participants, key regulatory changes, voting results, supporting Federal Register references, and emphasizes consistent, lawful, safe, and sound bank activities with appropriate risk controls.

This section records the Board of Governors’ 2023 policy actions and explains their statutory basis, categories, voting records, supporting sources, and relationship to the FOMC minutes. It covers capital requirements for banking organizations engaged in insurance, modernization of Community Reinvestment Act evaluations, administrative practice and procedure reforms, and additional rules concerning credit-loss allowances, commercial real estate workouts, and section 9(13) activity restrictions. The descriptions include effective dates, joint-agency participation, technical amendments and delayed provisions, regulatory objectives, votes, and Federal Register references, emphasizing lawful, fair, and safe and sound banking practices.

nodes.title: Policy Statements and Other Actions
Allowances for Credit Losses
nodes.summary: The passage records three unanimously approved 2023 Federal Reserve policy actions: an interagency update removing obsolete TDR references from credit-loss allowance guidance following CECL-related accounting changes; updated interagency guidance on commercial real estate loan workouts and short-term accommodations for financially stressed but creditworthy borrowers; and a section 9(13) policy establishing generally uniform activity limits for state member and national banks, including novel crypto-related activities, while requiring legal compliance, safe and sound operations, risk management, and internal controls. It identifies the approving officials and provides Federal Register references.

nodes.title: Commercial Real Estate Loan Accommodations and Workouts
nodes.summary: The text records three 2023 Board policy actions: an interagency update removing TDR references from credit-loss allowance guidance after adoption of CECL; updated interagency guidance on commercial real estate workouts and short-term loan accommodations during borrower stress; and a section 9(13) policy establishing generally consistent activity limits for state member and other Board-supervised banks, including crypto-related activities, while emphasizing legal compliance, safety and soundness, risk management, and internal controls. It also identifies the approving governors and provides Federal Register citations.

nodes.title: Policy Statement on Section 9(13) of the Federal Reserve Act
nodes.summary: The text records 2023 Board policy actions on credit-loss allowances, commercial real estate workouts and short-term accommodations, state-member-bank activity limits under section 9(13), climate-related financial-risk management, and emergency responses to the Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank failures. It explains the purpose and scope of each action, identifies voting outcomes, describes the systemic-risk exception and creation and legal basis of the Bank Term Funding Program, and provides related Federal Register and press-release references.

nodes.title: Principles for Climate-Related Financial Risk Management
nodes.summary: The text records Board action and voting on institutional information systems, describes the October 2023 interagency climate-related financial risk management principles for financial institutions with over $100 billion in assets, and details the March 2023 response to the failures of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank. That response included recommending the systemic risk exception to FDIC least-cost resolution rules and creating the emergency Bank Term Funding Program under section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act, whose lending authority requires Treasury approval and is subject to statutory limits.

nodes.title: Systemic Risk Exception and Bank Term Funding Program
nodes.summary: The text records Federal Reserve Board actions and votes concerning institutional information-system adequacy, climate-related financial-risk principles for institutions over $100 billion, the March 2023 systemic-risk exception recommendations and Bank Term Funding Program created during the SVB and Signature failures, and final interagency third-party-risk-management guidance. It explains the legal basis, purpose, eligibility, collateral, pricing, later rate modification, and scheduled closure of the BTFP; identifies supporting and dissenting governors for each action; and provides related regulatory and press-release references.

nodes.title: Third-Party Risk Management
nodes.summary: The text records Board actions concerning security requirements for insolvent entities, the creation and terms of the BTFP—including eligible borrowers, collateral, valuation, pricing, later rate modification, and scheduled end of new lending—and the associated votes. It also describes the Board’s June 2023 final interagency third-party risk-management guidance with the FDIC and OCC, its scope and principles, the supporting and opposing votes, and related source links.

nodes.title: Interest on Reserves
nodes.summary: The text records the Federal Reserve Board’s 2023 decisions on interest paid on reserve balances: three increases from 4.4% to 5.15% in February, March, and May, a hold in June, another increase to 5.4% in July, and holds at 5.4% in September, November, and December. Each action supported the corresponding FOMC federal funds target decision, and voting participants and press-release references are provided. It also explains that, under the Federal Reserve Act, Reserve Banks establish discount-window rates for depository institutions at least every 14 days subject to Board review; the Board considers proposals for primary credit rates and secondary and seasonal credit-rate formulas, with year-end rates in table E.1 and links to meeting minutes and historical rates.

This section records the Federal Reserve’s 2023 policy actions on credit-loss allowances, commercial real estate accommodations, Section 9(13) activity limits including crypto activities, climate-related financial-risk management, institutional information systems, third-party risk management, and security requirements. It details the systemic-risk response to the Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank failures, including the legal basis and operational terms of the Bank Term Funding Program. It also covers interest paid on reserve balances, discount-window rate-setting procedures, voting outcomes and officials, and supporting Federal Register, press-release, meeting-minute, and historical-rate references.

nodes.title: Discount Rates for Depository Institutions in 2023
Primary, Secondary, and Seasonal Credit
nodes.summary: The text presents year-end 2023 Federal Reserve lending rates and explains the primary, secondary, and seasonal credit programs. It records four primary-rate increases from 4.5% to 5.5%, the 50-basis-point secondary-credit spread and 6% year-end rate, and the 5.35% seasonal-credit rate based on biweekly money-market yields. It also describes 90-day primary-credit borrowing terms, summarizes Board approvals renewing rate formulas, and begins the account of votes on discount-rate changes, including the February 1, 2023, FOMC meeting and actions by several Reserve Bank boards.

nodes.title: Votes on Changes to Discount Rates for Depository Institutions
nodes.summary: The text reports year-end 2023 Federal Reserve lending rates and explains the purposes, eligibility, terms, and rate-setting methods for primary, secondary, and seasonal credit. It records the Board’s four 2023 increases in the primary credit rate—from 4.50% to 5.50%—including effective dates, participating Reserve Banks, voting officials, and approval timing, and notes the renewal of formulas for secondary and seasonal credit rates.

The section records the Board's late-2023 decisions to keep reserve-balance interest at 5.4 percent in support of the unchanged federal funds target, then explains the statutory and biweekly process for setting discount-window rates. It describes the primary, secondary, and seasonal credit programs and their year-end rates, terms, and formulas; documents four 2023 increases in the primary credit rate from 4.50 to 5.50 percent, the corresponding 6.00 percent secondary rate and 5.35 percent seasonal rate; and summarizes the related Reserve Bank proposals, Board approvals, effective dates, participating banks, officials' votes, and supporting references.

nodes.title: The Board of Governors and the Government Performance and Results Act
nodes.summary: The Board voluntarily follows the spirit of GPRA by publishing a multiyear strategic plan, annual performance plan, and annual performance report. Its 2020–23 strategic plan, issued December 27, 2019, sets priorities across five functional areas and balances mission-focused objectives with flexibility for emerging challenges. The annual plan allocates priorities and resources for yearly initiatives, while the annual report records accomplishments and promotes transparency. These processes support the Board’s ability to prioritize and communicate its most critical work, and the documents are publicly available on the Board’s website.

structure.summary: This section records the Board of Governors’ 2023 regulatory, policy, emergency, interest-rate, and discount-window actions, detailing their legal bases, objectives, procedures, effective dates, participating agencies and banks, voting outcomes, officials, and supporting public references. It covers banking capital and insurance, Community Reinvestment Act modernization, administrative reforms, credit-loss and commercial-real-estate measures, Section 9(13) and crypto restrictions, climate and technology risk management, security and third-party oversight, and the response to the Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank failures through the Bank Term Funding Program. It also explains reserve-balance interest and the primary, secondary, and seasonal credit programs, including 2023 discount-rate changes. Finally, it describes the Board’s strategic, annual planning, and performance-reporting practices under the spirit of GPRA and their role in prioritization, communication, accountability, and transparency.

structure.title: F Litigation
structure.summary: The text reports the Board of Governors’ 2023 litigation workload: 16 total cases, comprising 7 new matters and 9 carried over, matching 2022, with 11 pending at year-end. It identifies 11 pending matters involving master-account challenges, Regulation II debit-interchange-fee challenges, a bank-acquisition review, contract and debt-collection claims, and Freedom of Information Act requests. It also describes five resolved cases, including stipulated dismissals, dismissal of a Regulation II challenge, and appellate affirmance of the Board’s prohibition orders.

structure.title: G Statistical Tables
structure.summary: Appendix G compiles 13 statistical tables documenting Federal Reserve securities operations, asset holdings, reserve requirements, banking offices, reserve-fund factors, commercial-bank balance sheets, margin regulations, Reserve Bank financial condition, income and expenses, historical financial trends, operational processing volumes, staffing and salaries, and real-estate costs and values. The tables cover monthly, annual, year-end, and long historical periods, provide data by Reserve Bank and bank class where applicable, and include notes defining measurements, collateral, accounting treatments, regulatory changes, revisions, rounding, and unavailable data, together with references to related Federal Reserve sources.
